The Williamson synthesis joins an **alkoxide** to an **alkyl halide** by an **SN2**
displacement, and SN2 sets the limit: the halide must be **methyl or primary**. A secondary
halide reacts poorly and a **tertiary** one not at all — the alkoxide, being a strong base as
well as a nucleophile, removes a β-hydrogen instead and the halide **eliminates** to an
alkene.
So the ether that cannot be made is the one requiring attack on a **tertiary** carbon from
**both** sides.
**(d) Di-tert-butyl ether** ✓ **cannot be made.** Either way round, the alkyl halide would
have to be tert-butyl halide, and (CH₃)₃C–X with an alkoxide gives isobutylene by E2, not the
ether.
The others can all be made, provided the right partner is chosen as the halide:
**(a) Methoxybenzene** — phenoxide + CH₃I. (Not the reverse: an aryl halide will not undergo
SN2, so the **phenol** must supply the alkoxide.)
**(b) Benzyl p-nitrophenyl ether** — p-nitrophenoxide + benzyl chloride, a primary halide.
**(c) Methyl tert-butyl ether** — tert-butoxide + **CH₃I**. The tertiary group comes from the
**alkoxide** side, where bulk is no obstacle, and the halide is methyl ✓ This is how MTBE is
made industrially.
The lesson in (c) and (d) together: a tertiary group is fine in the alkoxide, fatal in the
halide.

Two comparisons are needed: **carboxylic acids against phenols**, and then within each pair.
**Carboxylic acids are far more acidic than phenols.** A carboxylate ion spreads its negative
charge over **two equivalent oxygen atoms**, so both resonance structures are identical and
the stabilisation is large (pKa ≈ 4). A phenoxide spreads the charge into the **ring**, onto
carbon atoms that bear it much less comfortably (pKa ≈ 10). So
(III) and (IV) **≫** (I) and (II)
**Within the acids.** (III) is benzoic acid, pKa **4·20**; (IV) is p-toluic acid, pKa **4·37**.
The **–CH₃** group releases electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), which destabilises the
carboxylate, so p-toluic acid is the **weaker**:
(III) > (IV)
**Within the phenols.** (I) is phenol, pKa **10·0**; (II) is p-chlorophenol, pKa **9·4**. The
**–Cl** withdraws electrons (−I) and stabilises the phenoxide, so p-chlorophenol is the
**stronger**:
(II) > (I)
Putting all four together:
**(III) > (IV) > (II) > (I)** ✓
The pattern to carry away: an **electron-withdrawing** substituent strengthens an acid and an
**electron-releasing** one weakens it, whichever class of acid is involved — and the class
itself outweighs any substituent effect.
∴ (III) > (IV) > (II) > (I).

The starting material has **two** carbonyl groups — a **ketone** and an **ester** — and
ethylene glycol with acid is the standard way of **protecting** one of them as a cyclic
acetal (a 1,3-dioxolane).
**Which one is protected?** Only the **ketone**. An ester is far less electrophilic than a
ketone, because the lone pair on its –OR oxygen is delocalised into the carbonyl and reduces
the partial positive charge on the carbon. Esters therefore do **not** form acetals under
these conditions.
So the major product keeps the **–OC₂H₅** ester intact and carries a **five-membered
dioxolane ring** where the ketone was ✓ — which is option (b).
Now the others:
**(a)** shows the glycol simply added as a diol without closing the ring — not an acetal at
all.
**(c)** has the dioxolane formed but the ester hydrolysed to **–OH**; the acid is catalytic
and anhydrous, so no hydrolysis occurs.
**(d)** shows a four-membered ring; ethylene glycol has two carbons and forms a **five**-
membered 1,3-dioxolane, which is the ring size that closes most readily.
This selectivity is exactly why the reaction is used. The ketone is masked, some other
operation is carried out on the ester, and dilute aqueous acid then restores the ketone
unchanged.
∴ option (b).
